lines.text: Introduction, section three. Key concepts from volume one.
Before we dive into anything new, let us do a quick tour of the ideas from the first book that we are going to rely on heavily here.
The first idea is equilibrium: a pair of strategies where neither player can improve their expected value by unilaterally deviating.
The second is exploitability: a measure of how much expected value you are leaving on the table when you play something other than an equilibrium strategy against a perfect opponent.
Equilibrium strategies are unexploitable, which is what makes them a safe default when you do not have reliable reads on your opponent.

The third idea is the polarized versus condensed dynamic, where the polarized range holds either the nuts or bluffs, and the condensed range holds a lot of medium-strength hands that beat bluffs but lose to value bets.
Polarized ranges bet big and get to charge condensed ranges to see showdown; that asymmetry is where a huge amount of poker profit comes from.
The fourth idea is indifference, which we already met in the recurring hypothetical: at a mixed equilibrium, all the actions you mix between must have the same expected value.
Indifference is not a strange coincidence; it is the very thing that makes a mixed strategy stable.
If any one option were better, you would take it always, and your opponent would adjust.
The final idea to keep front of mind is the value of position: acting last gives you information, and information turns into expected value in almost every spot we will study.
If any of these still feel wobbly, the first book covers them in detail, and this book will assume you can pick them up on the fly.
